1:
The psalm announces itself as a puzzle before it announces a grievance. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that the word stands as a title only here and in one prophet’s prayer, and offers two readings: a wandering song, the matter and composition of its several parts differing though artificially put together, or a charming song, very delightful. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) derives it from a root meaning to wander and takes it for a psalm composed in David’s wanderings, when he was obliged to hide himself from the fury of Saul; he reports Bishop Horsley’s suggestion of a wandering ode, named from its taking up different subjects in different styles, and his own alternative of an unpremeditated song, an improviso. John Calvin (reformed) lists the Jewish opinions — a musical instrument, a tune, the opening of a common song whose air David borrowed — and prefers the second, some kind of melody or measure as one might speak of a Sapphic verse, adding that he will not contend about a matter of so small importance.

Who the Benjamite was divides the same three. Henry allows that Cush may be Saul himself, whose barbarous usage of David bespoke him rather a Cushite or an Ethiopian than a true-born Israelite, but thinks it more likely some kinsman of Saul so named, an inveterate enemy who misrepresented David as a traitor and needlessly exasperated the king against him. Clarke finds the man unknown in Jewish history and takes the name for a disguise covering Saul, the son of Kish and of the tribe of Benjamin. Calvin rejects the fiction outright: David names Saul plainly elsewhere, and paints him in colours no less black than he does here, so why suppress it here and not there; the accuser is a real man of Saul’s tribe, either bribed by the king or currying his favour, and the first verse describes David’s circumstances as a persecuted man while the second names the fountain of his calamity.

Two readings stand further off. Augustine of Hippo (latin-fathers) finds the occasion not in Saul’s reign but in the later revolt of David’s son, where the friend who crossed to the son’s side to report his designs bears this name; and, reading the names spiritually rather than carnally according to the letter, he reports interpreters who render Chusi as silence, Gemini as right-handed and Achitophel as a brother’s ruin, so that the traitor Judas meets us again in the figure, since the Lord calls his disciples both sons and brethren. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the heading as evidence rather than allegory: the psalm continues the confident theme of the one before it, abounds in unmistakeable references to the persecution under Saul, and carries one of those statements of occasion found only in Davidic psalms.

On the two verses themselves the pleas are counted and the lion identified. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) hears the case opened with an avowal of confidence: I shake, but my rock moves not; it is never right to distrust God, and never vain to trust him. He bids us pause before we pray, lest we offer the sacrifice of fools, and hears in the dread of being torn fear co-working with faith. Henry numbers four pleas — David’s relation to God, his confidence in God, the rage of his enemies and the failure of all other helpers — observes that it is the glory of God to help the helpless, and adds that Paul compares Nero to a lion as David here compares Saul. Calvin takes the figure as setting the cruelty of Saul in a stronger light, and ascribes to God as his peculiar province the rescue of his poor sheep from the jaws of wolves. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) would render the opening claim, in thee have I taken refuge.
3:
What David is accused of must be inferred, and the voices infer alike. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) states the charge as Saul laid it, that David was affecting the kingdom and waiting to take away the life of his king, his patron and his friend; David meets it with indignation and clears himself by an imprecation that, if he had meditated any such thing, nothing but curse and calamity might meet him from God or man. John Gill (reformed) observes that the crime was so public that everybody knew it and needed no particular mention, and reports the Targum turning the words upon the psalm itself: if I have made this song with an evil intention, to give an ill character of any. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the demonstrative to point to the substance of the Benjamite’s slanderous sayings, and set the line beside David’s own words to Saul that there is no evil in his hand, which shows in a small compass the difference between poetical and prose expression.

The counter-evidence is the sparing of Saul. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) answers the charge with the record: David had suffered his enemy to escape when he had him completely in his power, twice sparing Saul’s life, once in the cave and again when he found him sleeping in the midst of his slumbering camp, and could therefore appeal to heaven with a clear conscience. Clarke supplies the cave: David contented himself with cutting off the skirt, merely to show the king the danger he had been in and the spirit of the man he accused of designs against his life, and even for this his heart smote him, as an indignity offered to the Lord’s anointed. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) sees in those two notorious instances of magnanimity how closely the psalm is tied to that part of David’s life, and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) notes that the deliverance came when it was in his power to destroy him.

The verse carrying the counter-claim is held to be damaged. Ellicott reports that Ewald, on metrical grounds and to avoid the abrupt change of construction, conjectures that two clauses have dropped out, that Milton’s translation gives it another colour, and that the Greek and Latin support the supposition of corruption, so that a slight change yields the probable sense: if I have returned evil to him that dealt friendly with me, and injured my enemy without cause. Gill notes Jarchi’s alternative rendering, if I rewarded him as he rewarded me, evil for evil, which David did not.

The imprecation that follows is weighed as well as construed. Gill reads it plainly: if the charge could be proved, David was content that Saul should pursue, apprehend him, and take away his life. Ellicott would read an enemy rather than the enemy, renders the verb for persecute literally as burn, and finds the word for tread used of a potter treading clay, of trampling horses and of a herd treading down its pasture; honour he takes by the parallelism for the soul or life, though to lay one’s honour in the dust is a common figure; the pause mark he reads as a direction to the music to strike up with passion and force. Spurgeon holds that he needs not fear the curse whose soul is clear of guilt, yet calls the imprecation most solemn and justifiable only through the extremity of the occasion and the dispensation the psalmist lived under, since we are now commanded to let our yea be yea, and if we cannot be believed on our word we are not to be trusted on our oath, and he warns the unconverted against trifling with imprecations, instancing the woman who wished she might die if she had not paid her share, and fell dead with the money in her hand.
6:
Asking God to arise and awake raises a difficulty the voices meet. John Gill (reformed) denies that local motion is meant, which cannot belong to one infinite and immense, and takes the words as spoken after the manner of men, of a God who seems sometimes to have laid himself down unconcerned, taking no notice of the insults of the wicked. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) makes the figure sharper still: David’s sorrow makes him view the Lord as a Judge who had left the judgment-seat and retired into his rest, and the call to awake is bolder yet, implying sleep as well as inactivity and applicable to God only in a limited sense; his silence is the patience of longsuffering. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads it as a committal: to thee I commit my cause, arise and sit on the throne of thy judgment in my behalf. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) glosses the commanded judgment as the sentence God had appointed and declared by his prophet Samuel.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets a plea under each petition. Under the prayer for wrath he puts the enemies’ own: they are unjustly angry at me, be thou justly angry with them; those need not fear men’s wrath who have God’s wrath for them. The commanded judgment speaks both divine power and divine purpose: as God blesses effectually and is said to command the blessing, so he judges effectually, and though he seem to connive at wrong like one asleep he will awake in due time and make it appear that the delays were no neglects. The call to return on high he reads as a demand that God resume the royal throne whose sovereignty they had despised, and notes that some make it point to the resurrection and ascension of Christ, who on returning on high had all judgment committed to him, or to his second coming.

The scene the psalm imagines is read two ways. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes the clause as optative, let the communities of peoples be gathered round thee, and sees a vision in which Jehovah summons the nations, arranges them at his tribunal and then returns to his high throne to preside — which he prefers to Delitzsch’s departure into the height as a victor after battle; and the picture of arraigned nations he holds to favour making the psalm the voice of the community rather than of an individual. Gill keeps it national: the congregation is Israel’s twelve tribes, and he rejects the reading of several Jewish commentators who make them compass God in a hostile manner, taking it of Israel surrounding the altar with songs of deliverance.

The appeal to be judged by his own righteousness is the chapter’s hardest claim. Ellicott reports Jerome’s refusal of it to David at all, as belonging properly to the sinless Saviour, and the view of others that the ideal Israel stands at the tribunal; but he compares Job’s protestations of innocence and persistent demand for a trial, and holds that David refers to his innocence of the charge calumniously brought, since as between Saul and himself his conduct had been blameless. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hear in the strophe the calm language of courageous trust, and insist the prayer is directed not against the individuals as such but against the wickedness in them, which makes this psalm the key to all psalms containing prayers against enemies. Spurgeon has David’s hand on an honest heart and his cry to a righteous Judge, and marvels at the plea: how deep the divine knowledge, how intimate the search that tries the hearts, the secret thoughts, and the reins, the inward affections. Clarke asks only that his innocence be brought to light and his just dealing made clear as the noonday, and identifies the wickedness of the wicked as Saul’s own conduct.
10:
The turn from pleading to assurance rests on a disputed figure. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) hears an exclusive claim: not merely that God is his defender, but that he looks for defence in no other, his hope of shelter in danger being placed in God alone. On that he builds two confidences: God saves the upright in heart with an everlasting salvation, and he owns every righteous cause. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the Hebrew literally as my shield is upon God, comparing a place where the same construction makes God the shield-bearer. John Gill (reformed) prefers my shield is with God, and takes the shield for Christ, now with the Father as intercessor and advocate, opposing his blood and righteousness to all the accusations of Satan.

The next line is the psalm’s textual battlefield, fought out at length by Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian). He traces the sentence through the Chaldee, Vulgate, Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic, and through Coverdale, Cardmarden and the Genevan version, observing that the evidence on one side positively affirms that God is angry every day and on the other positively denies it, the mass of it supporting the denial. The corruption he lays at the Chaldee’s door, for adding the words with the wicked, which the English translators followed while printing them in italics as absent from the Hebrew; and since the same letters pointed one way mean God and pointed the other mean not, he would restore the sense as God judgeth the righteous, and is not angry every day — he is not always chiding, which is why several versions bring in patience and longsuffering. Ellicott knows the same versions and the same proposal to read and not for and God, but judges the change unnecessary, the two clauses answering to each other.

Those who keep the received reading build on it. Henry finds the wicked not to be envied: as God’s mercies are new every morning towards his people, so his anger is new every morning against the wicked, upon the fresh occasions their renewed transgressions give. He is angry with them even in the merriest of their days, and in the days of their devotion, for if they prosper it is in wrath, and if they pray their very prayers are an abomination. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) adds that God not only detests sin but is angry with those who continue to indulge in it, for we have no insensible and stolid God to deal with. Gill guards the other clause: not all who are thought righteous are such, nor is any man naturally righteous or righteous by his own obedience, but only those made so by the obedience of Christ.

The whetted sword is read as a warning rather than a sentence. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold that if God will in the end let his wrath break forth, he will not do it without having threatened it every day, making the ungodly feel his indignation beforehand to strike a wholesome terror into them; the subject of the condition is any ungodly person whatever, and of the main clause God, so that if a man does not repent the Lord will whet his sword. Gill insists the one who must turn is not God but the wicked man, who must repent until a change is wrought in his heart and life. Ellicott calls the Hebrew doubly idiomatic and would render it surely, he will again whet his sword, and notes that bent is literally trodden, the foot being used to bend the bow as archers use it still. Clarke takes the instruments of death for a prophecy of Saul’s tragical death, wounded by Philistine arrows and ending his woful days on his own keen sword; Ellicott reads them as arrows tipped with fire by wrapping them in burning tow.
14:
The closing picture is a birth. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) gives it as a false conception: the sinner’s head conceives the mischief, contrives it with art and keeps the plot close, while his heart travails with iniquity; but at the birth it proves falsehood, a cheat upon himself, a lie in his right hand: he cannot compass what he intended, nor, gaining his point, gain the satisfaction he promised himself. C.H. Spurgeon (puritan-evangelical) traces the parentage: the devil has had doings with him and the virus of evil is in him, so the child is worthy of its father, whose name of old was the father of lies. John Gill (reformed) keeps to the pain, that he is big with iniquity as a woman with child, uneasy till he commits it; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the figure as deep design and vigorous endeavour, restless till the mischief is accomplished. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) draws the principle: God’s judgments are not arbitrary but follow on sin as its consequence.

The second figure is a trap. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes the metaphor from pits dug in the earth and slightly covered with reeds, so as not to be discerned from solid ground, until the animal steps on them, the surface breaks, and he falls in; Saul laid his plans with artifice and executed them with zeal, and when he had, as he supposed, David’s grave digged, he fell in himself. He quotes Horne, that all the world acknowledges the equity of a sentence which inflicts on the guilty the punishment they intended for the innocent. Spurgeon notices what the work cost the digger: he stooped to the dirty work and did not fear to soil his hands, willing to work in a ditch if others might fall therein; such men hunt the godly as brute beasts, and will not give them the fair chase afforded the hare or the fox, but must secretly entrap them, being able neither to run them down nor shoot them down. Henry generalises: all sinners prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction.

The reversal is stated, then placed in history. Gill has what the man devised against others fall upon himself, as a just judgment from heaven. Clarke glosses the old word for the head as the scalp or crown, thinks it may refer to knocking a criminal on the head to deprive him of life, and adds that had scalping been known then he should have thought that barbarous custom was meant. Ellicott notes the English word here is retained from Coverdale and common in the Elizabethan age; and he records that Eusebius applied these verses to the overthrow of Maxentius by Constantine, who in preparing a bridge of boats had prepared the means of his own destruction.

The psalm ends in praise. Henry takes the righteousness to cover both halves of the psalm: the glory of that gracious protection under which God takes his afflicted people, and of the just vengeance with which he will pursue those who afflict them, sung to the Lord most high, who, when his enemies deal proudly, shows he is above them. Clarke celebrates both justice and mercy, and takes the name for the perfections of a Jehovah above all; he quotes the old Scotico-English psalter beginning here, that song falls to joy, and he who sings that name well has joy more than can be told. Gill grounds it in a precedent: righteousness displayed in vindicating the innocent and punishing the wicked, as when the king who ordered the Hebrew infants drowned was himself drowned with his host, and Israel sang. Spurgeon ends on the contrast, the bright jewel sparkling in a black foil, and leaves the slandered man a singer again, his harp unstrung for a little season and now sweeping its chords.
